19031-a-treatise-on-adulterations-of-foo:
Frederick Accum, operative chemist and member of academies and societies of arts and sciences in Europe, published this treatise in Philadelphia in 1820. It exhibits the fraudulent sophistication of bread, beer, wine, spirits, tea, coffee, cream, confectionery, vinegar, mustard, pepper, cheese, olive oil, pickles, and other articles of domestic economy, with methods of detecting them.

Accum aimed to put the unwary on guard against poisons and cheats at the table, giving easy tests a householder could use. His book helped start the fight for pure food, and its warnings shocked readers. Readers get a landmark of food safety writing, plain in method and fierce in tone, that shows how much fraud hid in ordinary shopping two centuries ago.
a-treatise-on-adulterations-of-food-and-: Friedrich Christian Accum, working chemist, shows the cheating mix-ins in food in this treatise, printed at Philadelphia in 1820. Its title lists the doctored forms of bread, beer, wine, strong drink, tea, coffee, cream, sweets, vinegar, mustard, pepper, cheese, olive oil, and pickles, with ways of spotting them. The preface aims to warn the unwary of goods tainted with stuffs bad for health.
